questions.stem: State the two transport processes by which small soluble molecules are absorbed.
questions.modelAnswer: Absorption occurs through diffusion and sometimes active transport.

questions.stem: Name the two destinations of absorbed digested molecules.
questions.modelAnswer: They enter the blood, carrying glucose and amino acids, and the lymph, carrying fatty acids and glycerol.

questions.stem: Explain why fatty acids and glycerol take a different route from glucose.
questions.modelAnswer: Because they are absorbed into the lacteal, the lymph vessel at each villus's centre, which carries them in the lymph before they eventually join the blood; the lipid products' route differs from the sugar and amino-acid route through the capillaries.

questions.stem: A patient with severe intestinal damage absorbs glucose poorly. Suggest which transport mechanism has failed.
questions.modelAnswer: Diffusion may still passively move some glucose, but the active-transport component that tops up uptake against the gradient has likely failed, so total absorption falls short even when the luminal concentration favours movement.

questions.stem: State three adaptations of the small intestine for absorption.
questions.modelAnswer: It is very long, highly folded, and lined with millions of villi — all raising surface area.

questions.stem: Name the vessel that transports fats away from a villus.
questions.modelAnswer: The lacteal, a lymph vessel at the villus's centre, transports the fats.

questions.stem: Explain why fast drainage of the villus speeds absorption.
questions.modelAnswer: Because capillaries and the lacteal sweep absorbed molecules away the moment they cross, the inside of the villus never fills up, so the concentration gradient between the gut lumen and the villus interior stays steep and diffusion continues rapidly.

questions.stem: Coeliac disease flattens the villi. Predict the digestive consequence.
questions.modelAnswer: With the villi flattened, the absorbing surface collapses, the diffusion distance effectively rises, and malabsorption follows — less glucose, amino acids and fats cross into the blood and lymph, so the patient loses nourishment from an otherwise digested meal.
